posts.title: Sportsbooks Don't Gamble. You Do.
posts.text:
A sportsbook doesn't need to know who wins. We break down the hidden cut in every bet with a simple coin flip, show why parlays are the sportsbook's favorite product, and look at how much US sportsbooks actually kept in 2025.

Bet $110 to win $100 on both sides of a coin flip: the book takes in $220, pays out $210 and keeps $10, whoever wins. That's about 4.5 cents per dollar. On a five-leg parlay the same pricing takes about 21%. In 2025, Americans bet $166.94 billion on sports and sportsbooks kept $16.96 billion, about 10 cents of every dollar.

Episode 1 of How They Take Your Money.

posts.title: The Parlay Is the Sportsbook's Favorite Bet #shorts
posts.text:
Combine five coin-flip bets into one $10 parlay. A fair price would pay $320. The sportsbook pays about $254. The cut grows with every bet you add: 4.5% on one bet, about 21% on five. In 2025, Americans bet $166.94 billion on sports and sportsbooks kept $16.96 billion, about 10 cents of every dollar.
Source: American Gaming Association (2026). Parlay figures: simplified example at -110 odds.

posts.title: What Happens If You Keep Winning at Sports Betting? #shorts
posts.text:
Sportsbooks can limit players who win, by lowering how much they're allowed to bet. In Massachusetts, 0.64% of sports betting accounts were limited in some way, and the state's sports betting chief confirmed that winning players tend to get their limits lowered and losing players get them raised.
Source: Massachusetts Gaming Commission data (2024-2025).

posts.title: Sportsbooks Don't Care Who Wins #shorts
posts.text:
The sportsbook's cut is hidden in the odds: both sides of an even game add up to about 105%. If too much money lands on one team, the book moves the odds until money comes in on both sides again. It doesn't need to know who wins. It just needs both sides busy, and then it sells you the parlay.
(Simplified example at standard -110 odds.)

Full explanation: the related video linked above.
